title: Pteridophyta — Ferns and Allies
topicTitle: Pteridophyta: General introduction and characteristic features of pteridophytes; morphological structure and reproduction of Dryopteris; economic importance of pteridophytes
notes: **General features of Pteridophyta:** First vascular plants — possess true xylem (tracheids only, no vessel elements) and phloem (sieve tubes with companion cells). Have true roots (adventitious), stems (rhizomes), and leaves (fronds/megaphylls). Reproduce by spores (not seeds). Dominant sporophyte generation (diploid, 2n) is the large, conspicuous plant. Gametophyte (haploid, n) is small, independent, and free-living (called prothallus). Require water for fertilisation — antheridial sperm are flagellated and must swim to archegonia. Spores have sporopollenin walls resistant to desiccation and UV radiation.

**Classes of Pteridophyta:** Psilopsida (most primitive, no true roots, e.g., Psilotum — 2 species); Lycopsida (club mosses, microphylls — small leaves with single vein, e.g., Selaginella ~800 species, Lycopodium ~400 species); Sphenopsida (horsetails, jointed hollow stems, reduced scale leaves at nodes, e.g., Equisetum ~15 species); Pteropsida (true ferns, megaphylls — large leaves with branching veins, e.g., Dryopteris, Pteris, Nephrolepis — ~12,000 species). Psilopsida and Lycopsida are primarily tropical; Sphenopsida is cosmopolitan but sparse; Pteropsida is the largest and most diverse class.

**Dryopteris — morphological structure:** (a) Rhizome: underground, horizontal stem (creeping rhizome) with central pith surrounded by a ring of vascular bundles (dictyostele). Covered with brown, scale-like hairs (trichomes) for protection. (b) Adventitious roots: arise from the lower surface of the rhizome, branching, without root caps (typical of pteridophytes). (c) Fronds (leaves): large, compound leaves arising from the rhizome tip. Young fronds are coiled in circinate vernation (fiddlehead). Mature fronds are pinnately compound with numerous pinnae (leaflets). (d) Sori: clusters of sporangia on the undersurface of fertile pinnae, protected by a kidney-shaped indusium (flap of tissue).

**Vascular tissue in pteridophytes:** Xylem contains only tracheids (elongated, tapered cells with lignified secondary walls and pits for water conduction) — no vessel elements (which appear in gymnosperms and angiosperms). Phloem contains sieve tubes (conducting cells) and companion cells (metabolically supportive) — no albuminous cells (found in gymnosperms). The absence of vessels is a primitive characteristic. In Dryopteris, the stele is a dictyostele: a hollow cylinder of vascular tissue with gaps (leaf gaps) where vascular traces diverge to each frond.

**Stele types in pteridophytes:** Protostele — solid central vascular cylinder with no pith (e.g., Rhynia, Psilotum, Selaginella). Siphonostele — vascular tissue forms a ring around a central pith (e.g., Marsilea, Cyathea). Dictyostele — a siphonostele with multiple vascular traces branching off to leaves, leaving gaps in the cylinder (e.g., Dryopteris, most mature ferns). The evolutionary trend is protostele → siphonostele → dictyostele, reflecting increasing complexity of leaf evolution and vascular supply.

**Sporangium types in pteridophytes:** Eusporangium — develops from multiple epidermal cells, has a thick multi-layered wall, is large (0.2-0.5 mm), and produces many spores (e.g., Ophioglossum, Psilotum, Marsilea). Leptosporangium — develops from a single epidermal cell, has a thin single-layered wall, is small (0.1-0.2 mm), and produces fewer spores (e.g., Dryopteris, Pteris, Lycopodium). Leptosporangia are more derived and efficient — the annulus (see below) is a leptosporangiate innovation that acts as a mechanical catapult for spore dispersal.

**Dryopteris sporangium structure:** Each sporangium sits on a short stalk (annulus is part of the stalk region). The annulus consists of 8-10 thick-walled, tangentially elongated cells arranged in a curved row — this is the dehiscence mechanism. Beneath the annulus is a ring of thin-walled cells (annulus cap). The sporangium wall (jacket) is a single layer of sterile cells. Inside is sporogenous tissue that undergoes meiosis to produce 64 haploid spores. When the sporangium matures, the annulus cells lose water by transpiration through their thin outer walls. The thick inner walls resist shrinking, creating tension. When tension exceeds a threshold, the annulus snaps back (like a released spring), the sporangium wall ruptures, and spores are catapulted outward — a passive mechanical dispersal mechanism.

**Reproduction in Dryopteris — homosporous life cycle:** Dryopteris is homosporous — all spores are identical in size and type. A spore (n) germinates on moist soil → produces a prothallus (small, green, photosynthetic, heart-shaped gametophyte, 5-15 mm across). The prothallus bears rhizoids on its ventral surface for water absorption. Antheridia (male organs) develop on the ventral surface, typically near the anterior notch. Each antheridium is a globular structure with a sterile jacket surrounding androphores (sterile cells) and spermatogenous tissue. Archegonia (female organs) develop between the antheridia, typically on the ventral surface. Each archegonium has a neck (2 neck canal cells), a venter (1 venter canal cell + 1 egg cell), and a jacket. Water is required for antherozoids to swim to the archegonium.

**Prothallus — the gametophyte generation:** The prothallus is a free-living, independent, photosynthetic structure. It is NOT dependent on the sporophyte for nutrition (unlike bryophyte gametophytes, which are independent, and unlike bryophyte sporophytes, which are dependent — this reversal is a key evolutionary advancement). The prothallus is hermaphrodite (bisexual) — it bears both antheridia and archegonia. However, spatial and temporal separation reduces self-fertilisation: antheridia typically mature before archegonia on the same prothallus (protandry), and a chemical signal from mature archegonia inhibits nearby antheridium development (promoting outcrossing). Rhizoids also absorb water and minerals from the substrate.

**Sex determination and outcrossing in prothallus:** A prothallus with mature archegonia produces a hormone (antheridiogen) that suppresses antheridium development in nearby prothalli, while promoting it in distant ones. This ensures that a prothallus with archegonia will be fertilised by sperm from a different prothallus (cross-fertilisation), maintaining genetic diversity. This is an evolutionary innovation towards avoiding inbreeding — a key advantage of the independent sporophyte generation becoming dominant. Without this mechanism, self-fertilisation on the same prothallus would reduce genetic variation.

**Heterospory in pteridophytes — evolutionary significance:** Some pteridophytes (Selaginella, Marsilea, Salvinia) are heterosporous — they produce two types of spores: microspores (small, male) in microsporangia, and megaspores (large, female) in megasporangia. Microspores develop into reduced male gametophytes (few cells) that remain within the microspore wall. Megaspores develop into larger female gametophytes that retain the spore wall. This is a critical evolutionary step toward the seed habit: retention of the megaspore on the parent sporophyte + development of an integument (protective layer) around it = ovule formation. The seed habit was completed in gymnosperms, making heterospory a key transitional innovation.

**Dryopteris frond development (circinate vernation):** Young fronds emerge from the rhizome tip coiled tightly like a fiddlehead (crozier). The tip of the frond is at the centre of the coil. As the frond unfurls, the tip uncoils first, and the base follows — this is circinate vernation. The vascular trace in each leaf connects to the rhizome stele. The coiled young frond protects the delicate growing tip from desiccation and mechanical damage. This is a diagnostic feature of most leptosporangiate ferns. In Nepal, young fiddleheads (called 'pidne' in Nepali) are eaten as a vegetable.

**Psilotum — the most primitive pteridophyte:** Lacks true roots (has rhizomes with mycorrhizal fungi) and true leaves (has enations — small outgrowths without vascular tissue). Photosynthetic green stems with sporangia borne in clusters of three (trirs). The sporangium is trilocular (three-chambered) and dehisces by longitudinal slits. Psilotum has a symbiotic mycorrhizal association with fungi (similar to orchids), suggesting it lost roots during evolution rather than never having them. It represents an early stage in vascular plant evolution and is found in tropical regions (Caribbean, Japan, New Zealand).

**Equisetum (horsetail) — living relic:** The only surviving genus of Sphenopsida. Jointed hollow stems with silica deposited in cell walls (giving stems a rough, abrasive texture — used as 'scouring rush' for polishing). Reduced scale-like leaves arranged in whorls at nodes. Sporangia borne in cone-like strobili at stem tips (not scattered on fronds like Dryopteris). Spores have four elater-like appendages (sterile, hygroscopic threads) that aid dispersal. Equisetum arvense (field horsetail) is a common weed in temperate regions; E. giganteum grows up to 2 m tall. Fossil relatives (Calamites) were giant trees (30+ m) in Carboniferous swamps.

**Selaginella — spikemoss with heterospory:** ~800 species, mostly tropical. Stem-like axis with overlapping microphyllous leaves. Produces strobili (cones) at stem tips containing sporangia. Microsporangia produce many small microspores (male); megasporangia produce 4 large megaspores (female). The male gametophyte develops entirely within the microspore wall (highly reduced). The female gametophyte develops within the megaspore wall, retaining nutrients. This 'endomitic' development (gametophyte inside spore wall) is a key step toward the seed habit — the megaspore is retained on the parent plant rather than being dispersed immediately.

**Marsilea (water fern / clover fern):** Aquatic heterosporous pteridophyte. Four leaflets arranged like a clover (hence 'clover fern'). Sporocarps (hard, protective, spherical structures) borne on stalks arise from the rhizome. Each sporocarp contains both microsporangia and megasporangia (in separate locules). Microspores develop into male gametophytes; megaspores into female gametophytes. The sporocarp wall protects spores during dry periods — an adaptation to intermittent aquatic habitats. In Nepal, Marsilea quadrifolia is found in rice fields and slow-moving water. The sporocarps are edible and nutritious when roasted.

**Economic importance of pteridophytes:** (1) Ornamental: Dryopteris, Nephrolepis (Boston fern), Adiantum (maidenhair fern), Platycerium (staghorn fern) are popular houseplants. (2) Soil erosion control: ground-cover ferns stabilise slopes and prevent soil loss on hillsides (important in Nepal's mountainous terrain). (3) Medicinal: Dryopteris filix-mas (male fern) contains filicin — an effective anthelmintic against tapeworms. Equisetum species are used in traditional medicine for kidney disorders and wound healing (silica content). (4) Biofertilizer: Azolla (floating fern) symbiotically associates with Anabaena (cyanobacterium) in its cavities; fixes atmospheric nitrogen; used as green manure in rice paddies (2-3 tonnes N/ha per crop cycle). (5) Food: young fiddleheads (Dryopteris, Osmunda) are edible vegetables in Japan and Nepal. (6) Geological: Carboniferous pteridophytes formed the world's coal deposits (80%+ of coal).

**Pteridophyte adaptations to terrestrial life:** Cuticle on epidermis reduces water loss (though less developed than in seed plants). Stomata on sporophyte tissues (some hornworts and ferns) for gas exchange. True roots with rhizoids for water and mineral absorption from soil. Vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) enables long-distance transport of water, minerals, and photosynthates. Spores with sporopollenin walls resist desiccation, UV radiation, and microbial attack — enabling dispersal through dry air. These adaptations allowed pteridophytes to colonise diverse terrestrial habitats, though water dependency for fertilisation still limits them to moist environments.

**Ferns in the fossil record and coal formation:** Pteridophytes dominated Earth's vegetation during the Carboniferous period (360-290 million years ago), forming vast swamp forests. Giant club mosses (Lepidodendron — up to 50 m tall) and giant horsetails (Calamites — up to 30 m tall) died, accumulated in swampy conditions, and were buried under sediment. Over millions of years, heat and pressure converted this organic matter into coal. Over 80% of the world's coal reserves are Carboniferous pteridophyte-derived. The word 'Carboniferous' literally means 'coal-bearing.' Modern pteridophytes are smaller and less dominant but retain these ancient features.

**Fern allergy and spore sensitivity:** Some people are allergic to pteridophyte spores, particularly from common garden ferns like Nephrolepis and Platycerium. The spores are extremely lightweight (15-50 micrometres), easily become airborne, and contain proteins that can trigger respiratory allergies (rhinitis, asthma) in sensitive individuals. This is not a toxicity issue but an immune response. People working with large fern collections or in greenhouses may develop 'fern worker's lung' — a form of hypersensitivity pneumonitis. The spores themselves are not poisonous but can cause contact dermatitis in some species.

**Fern hormones and plant growth regulation:** Pteridophytes produce auxins, cytokinins, and gibberellins — the same classes of plant hormones found in flowering plants. The first cytokinin (zeatin) was isolated from corn kernels but was first identified in herring sperm DNA — however, the understanding of cytokinin activity was greatly advanced by studies on fern prothalli. Fern gametophytes are used in research to study cell differentiation, pattern formation, and hormone interactions because the haploid prothallus is genetically uniform and easy to culture. These studies contributed to the broader field of plant physiology.

**Ecological role of ferns:** Epiphytic ferns in tropical rainforests (e.g., Platycerium, Asplenium) grow on tree branches, capturing moisture and nutrients from the air and creating microhabitats for invertebrates, amphibians, and microorganisms. Ground-cover ferns (e.g., Dryopteris, Polypodium) stabilise forest floors, reduce erosion, and maintain soil moisture. In Nepal's mid-hills, Dryopteris species form dense ground cover in rhododendron and oak forests, preventing landslides during monsoon. Azolla in rice fields fixes atmospheric nitrogen (up to 60 kg N/ha per season), reducing fertiliser costs for farmers. Ferns also serve as food for herbivorous insects and caterpillars.
confusion:
❌ Ferns are the same as mosses.
✅ Ferns (pteridophytes) have vascular tissue (xylem with tracheids, phloem with sieve tubes) while mosses (bryophytes) lack vascular tissue entirely. Ferns have a dominant sporophyte generation (the visible leafy plant) with independent gametophyte (prothallus). Mosses have a dominant gametophyte generation (the visible green plant) with dependent sporophyte. Ferns can grow tall (due to vascular support); mosses remain low-growing (a few cm). Both require water for fertilisation, but ferns have true roots, stems, and leaves while mosses have rhizoids and phyllids.

❌ Pteridophytes reproduce by seeds.
✅ Pteridophytes reproduce by spores, NOT seeds. Seeds are a derived feature of gymnosperms and angiosperms — they consist of a dormant embryo, stored food, and a protective coat. Pteridophyte spores are single cells (haploid, n) that germinate into free-living gametophytes. The presence of vascular tissue but absence of seeds is what distinguishes pteridophytes from gymnosperms (which have naked seeds) and angiosperms (which have enclosed seeds). Spores are dispersed individually; seeds contain an embryo ready to grow.

❌ All pteridophytes are homosporous (produce one spore type).
✅ While most pteridophytes (including Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum) are homosporous (one spore type → bisexual gametophyte), several important groups are heterosporous: Selaginella (spikemoss), Marsilea (water fern), and Salvinia (water fern). Heterospory (two spore types: microspores and megaspores) is an evolutionary advancement that led toward the seed habit. Assuming all pteridophytes are homosporous is a common oversight — heterospory is rare but phylogenetically critical.

❌ The prothallus is the sporophyte generation.
✅ The prothallus is the GAMETOPHYTE generation (haploid, n) — it is small, heart-shaped, and independent. It produces gametes (sperm and egg) in antheridia and archegonia. The sporophyte is the large, leafy fern plant (diploid, 2n) that we commonly recognise as a 'fern.' This is the reverse of bryophytes, where the gametophyte is dominant and the sporophyte is small and dependent. The independence of the pteridophyte sporophyte is a major evolutionary advancement over bryophytes.

❌ The indusium is a type of spore or part of the leaf blade.
✅ The indusium is a flap or shield of protective tissue that covers and shelters the sorus (cluster of sporangia) on the underside of a fertile frond. It is modified leaf tissue (epidermis) that tears open when spores mature, exposing the sporangia. It is NOT a spore, NOT part of the photosynthetic blade, and NOT a reproductive organ itself — it is a protective covering for the sporangia. In Dryopteris, the indusium is kidney-shaped (reniform) and attached at one point.

❌ The annulus is just a ring of ordinary cells.
✅ The annulus is a specialised structure of 8-10 thick-walled, tangentially elongated cells that function as a mechanical catapult for spore dispersal. When the annulus loses water, the thick inner walls resist shrinking while the thin outer walls contract, creating elastic tension. When the tension exceeds a threshold, the annulus snaps back to its original position, rupturing the sporangium wall and catapulting spores outward. This active dispersal mechanism (drying-triggered mechanical action) is unique to leptosporangiate ferns and is not found in mosses or liverworts.

❌ Azolla is a moss or algae used in rice fields.
✅ Azolla is a FLOATING FERN (Pteridophyta, Marsileaceae), not a moss or algae. It forms a symbiotic relationship with the cyanobacterium Anabaena (also called Axonoglena) housed in cavities within its dichotomously branched fronds. Anabaena fixes atmospheric nitrogen (N2 → NH3) using the enzyme nitrogenase, which is oxygen-sensitive — Azolla's cavities provide the anaerobic environment needed. The fixed nitrogen is transferred to Azolla, which in turn fertilises rice paddies when the fern is incorporated into the soil. One crop cycle can fix 20-30 kg N/ha.

❌ Circinate vernation is unique to ferns and never occurs in other plants.
✅ Circinate vernation (coiled young leaf unfurling from the tip) is a hallmark of ferns and is particularly pronounced in them, but it also occurs in some cycads, palms (e.g., Coco de mer), and even some angiosperms (e.g., banana, protea). However, in ferns it is most consistent and diagnostic — nearly all leptosporangiate ferns show circinate vernation. The coiled fiddlehead protects the delicate apical meristem during emergence. In Nepal, young Dryopteris fiddleheads are harvested as a seasonal vegetable called 'pidne.'

❌ All pteridophytes have the same type of sporangium.
✅ Pteridophytes have two sporangium types: eusporangium (thick-walled, multi-cell origin, large, produces many spores — e.g., Ophioglossum, Marsilea) and leptosporangium (thin-walled, single-cell origin, small, produces fewer spores, has annulus for active dispersal — e.g., Dryopteris, Pteris, Lycopodium). Leptosporangia are more derived and efficient. Confusing the two types leads to misidentification of fern families. The presence of an annulus is the key diagnostic feature of leptosporangiate ferns.
practice: **Q1:** Draw and label the life cycle of Dryopteris, showing the alternation between sporophyte and gametophyte generations. Mark where meiosis and fertilisation occur. *Solution:* Draw two main phases connected in a cycle: (A) Sporophyte phase (2n, dominant): Large fern plant with rhizome, roots, fronds. Underside of fronds shows sori (brown clusters). Each sorus has indusium covering sporangia. Inside each sporangium: sporogenous tissue undergoes meiosis → produces haploid spores (n). Spores are released. (B) Gametophyte phase (n, independent): Spore germinates → prothallus (heart-shaped, green, 5-15 mm). Ventral surface has rhizoids, antheridia (male), and archegonia (female). Antheridium releases biflagellate antherozoids. Water required for swimming. Fertilisation: antherozoid + egg → zygote (2n) in archegonium. Zygote → embryo → new sporophyte. Arrows: spore(n) → prothallus(n) → gametes(n) → zygote(2n) → sporophyte(2n) → spores(n). Meiosis occurs in sporangia (sporophyte → spores). Fertilisation occurs in archegonium (gametophyte → zygote).

**Q2:** Compare and contrast the sporophyte of Dryopteris with the sporophyte of Marchantia (a bryophyte). Focus on vascular tissue, dominance, and dependence. *Solution:* VASCULAR TISSUE: Dryopteris sporophyte has true xylem (tracheids) and phloem (sieve tubes + companion cells) — can transport water and nutrients over long distances. Marchantia sporophyte has NO vascular tissue — relies on direct diffusion and nutrient transfer from gametophyte. DOMINANCE: Dryopteris sporophyte is the dominant, large, independent, long-lived generation (the visible fern plant, up to 1 m). Marchantia sporophyte is small, short-lived, and permanently attached to the gametophyte. DEPENDENCE: Dryopteris sporophyte is fully independent (photosynthesises, absorbs water/minerals via roots). Marchantia sporophyte is nutritionally dependent — foot absorbs sugars and water from the gametophyte archegoniophore. This contrast shows the evolutionary trend: bryophyte (gametophyte dominant, sporophyte dependent) → pteridophyte (sporophyte dominant, gametophyte independent).

**Q3:** Explain why heterospory is considered an evolutionary stepping stone to the seed habit. Use Selaginella as an example. *Solution:* Heterospory produces two spore types: microspores (male, small) and megaspores (female, large). In Selaginella, microspores develop into reduced male gametophytes (2-4 cells) within the spore wall. Megaspores develop into larger female gametophytes that retain the spore wall and nutrients. This retention of the megaspore on the parent sporophyte (instead of immediate dispersal) is the first step toward the seed habit. Next evolutionary steps: (1) integument (protective layer) grows around the megaspore → ovule; (2) the megaspore is fertilised while retained → seed with embryo and food supply. Selaginella shows the transition: megaspore retention + protected female gametophyte = precursor to the seed. Gymnosperms completed this transition; angiosperms added the fruit.

**Q4:** A student observes a plant with fronds and sori on the underside. Is it a bryophte or pteridophyte? Give three reasons for your identification. *Solution:* It is a PTERIDOPHYTE. Reason 1: Presence of sori (clusters of sporangia) on the underside of fronds is diagnostic of pteridophytes (specifically leptosporangiate ferns). Bryophytes do not produce sori — they produce sporangia (capsules) on setae (mosses) or embedded in gametophyte tissue (liverworts/hornworts). Reason 2: Fronds (compound, large leaves) indicate vascular tissue for structural support and transport — bryophytes lack true leaves and vascular tissue. Reason 3: The visible plant is the sporophyte (large, leafy, dominant generation), which is characteristic of pteridophytes. In bryophytes, the visible plant is the gametophyte (small, low-growing), and the sporophyte is a small stalk with a capsule. Additional evidence: pteridophyte spores have sporopollenin walls; bryophyte spores do not (or have thinner walls).

**Q5:** Why is Azolla used as a biofertilizer in rice fields? Explain the symbiotic relationship and the mechanism of nitrogen fixation. *Solution:* Azolla is a floating fern that forms a symbiotic cavity-dwelling relationship with the cyanobacterium Anabaena (Nostocales). Anabaena lives in the dorsal cavity of Azolla's bifurcated fronds. Anabaena possesses the enzyme nitrogenase, which converts atmospheric N2 into ammonia (NH3) — a form of nitrogen plants can use. Nitrogenase is oxygen-sensitive, so Anabaena differentiates some cells into heterocysts (thick-walled, oxygen-excluded cells) where nitrogen fixation occurs. Azolla provides Anabaena with photosynthates (sugars) and a protected, moist, anaerobic environment. In return, fixed nitrogen (up to 60 kg N/ha per crop cycle) is released into the rice paddy when Azolla is incorporated into the soil or dies. This reduces fertiliser costs by 30-50% for rice farmers in Nepal and India.

**Q6:** Describe the structure and function of the annulus in a Dryopteris sporangium. How does it aid in spore dispersal? *Solution:* Structure: The annulus is a curved row of 8-10 specialised cells at the junction between the sporangium capsule and the stalk. These cells have thick inner and radial walls but thin outer (anticlinal) walls. The annulus is positioned laterally, not at the tip. Function (dehiscence mechanism): When the sporangium matures, water evaporates through the thin outer walls of annulus cells. The thick inner walls resist shrinking, causing the annulus to bend backward (like a pulled spring). Tension builds until a critical point is reached, then the annulus snaps back to its original position. This rapid movement ruptures the sporangium wall, and the stored elastic energy catapults the spores outward (up to 10 cm distance). After discharge, the annulus slowly rehydrates and returns to its original position, ready for the next cycle. This mechanical dispersal is more efficient than passive spore release in bryophytes.

**Q7:** Differentiate between protostele, siphonostele, and dictyostele with suitable examples. Which type is found in Dryopteris? *Solution:* Protostele: solid central vascular cylinder with no pith. Simplest stele type. Found in Rhynia (extinct), Psilotum, and Selaginella. Siphonostele: vascular tissue forms a ring around a central pith (ground tissue). More complex; found in Marsilea (intermediate siphonostele with no leaf gaps) and Cyathea (tree fern, complete siphonostele). Dictyostele: a siphonostele modified by leaf gaps — vascular traces branch off from the central ring to supply each leaf, leaving gaps in the cylinder. The remaining vascular tissue forms narrow strands (carinal bundles) connected by medullary strands. Found in Dryopteris and most mature ferns. DICTYOSTELE is found in Dryopteris — the rhizome cross-section shows a ring of vascular bundles with gaps where frond traces diverge.

**Q8:** Compare homosporous and heterosporous pteridophytes. Give two examples of each and explain the evolutionary significance of heterospory. *Solution:* HOMOSPORY: one spore type, all spores identical in size and morphology, all develop into bisexual (monoecious) gametophytes bearing both antheridia and archegonia. Examples: Dryopteris (leptosporangiate fern), Pteris ( brake fern). HETEROSPORY: two spore types — microspores (small, numerous, develop into male gametophytes) and megaspores (large, few, develop into female gametophytes). Examples: Selaginella (spikemoss, terrestrial), Marsilea (water fern, aquatic). EVOLUTIONARY SIGNIFICANCE: Heterospory represents a critical transition toward the seed habit. Megaspore retention on the parent sporophyte (instead of immediate dispersal) allows the developing female gametophyte to receive nutrients from the parent. This is the precursor to the ovule (megaspore + integument + retained gametophyte). The male gametophyte being reduced and contained within the microspore wall parallels pollen grain structure in seed plants. Thus, heterospory is a key innovation bridging spore-bearing pteridophytes and seed-bearing gymnosperms.
universalFacts: Pteridophytes are the first plants to evolve true vascular tissue (xylem and phloem), enabling them to grow taller than bryophytes.

The sporophyte generation became dominant in pteridophytes — this is a major evolutionary trend: bryophytes (gametophyte dominant) → pteridophytes (sporophyte dominant) → seed plants (highly reduced gametophyte).
Sporopollenin, the most durable organic polymer known, protects pteridophyte spores from desiccation and UV radiation — it is also found in pollen grains of seed plants.
Dryopteris is one of the most common genera of ferns worldwide, found in temperate and tropical forests. Its fronds can reach 1 meter in length.
The study of pteridophytes is called 'ptérology' — a specialized branch of botany with over 12,000 living species worldwide.
